title: 22. Interview: What is Load Balancer?
summary: Interview Q&A for What is Load Balancer? — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 What is Load Balancer? interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What problem does a load balancer solve, and why is "just buy a bigger server" not a viable alternative?
**Answer:** A load balancer solves three problems at once: availability (one server dying should not take the product down), scalability (capacity should grow with the fleet, not with the box), and performance (requests should land on the fastest or least-loaded backend). "Just buy a bigger server" — vertical scaling — works up to a ceiling, but no single machine today can absorb the millions of concurrent connections a service like Netflix or Amazon receives. It also creates a single point of failure: when that one mega-box crashes, the product is down until you re-provision. Vertical scaling has a cost curve that goes vertical too — the largest EC2 instance is roughly 4× the price of a mid-size instance for 2× the CPU. Horizontal scaling behind a load balancer, by contrast, is linear in cost, has no upper bound, and survives individual node failures transparently. Real-world: Netflix runs thousands of small EC2 instances behind NGINX, not a few giant ones, precisely because the math and the availability math both favor horizontal.
**Visual:**
```
Vertical (one big box):        Horizontal (fleet behind LB):
+-------------------+          +------+   +------+
|   mega-server     |          | LB   |-->| B1   |
|  CPU: 448 vCPU    |          +------+   | B2   |
|  RAM: 6 TB        |                     | B3   |
|  $$$$ / single    |                     | B4   |
|  point of failure |                     | ...  |
+-------------------+                     +------+
```

### Q2. What is the difference between a hardware load balancer and a software load balancer, and why has the industry moved to software?
**Answer:** Hardware load balancers (F5 BIG-IP, Citrix NetScaler) are purpose-built appliances with custom ASICs that terminate millions of connections per second, sold as physical boxes with a fixed capacity and a months-long procurement cycle. Software load balancers (NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, AWS ELB) run on commodity servers or as managed cloud services, configured via YAML or API, and can be deployed in minutes. The industry moved to software for three reasons: operational velocity (config-as-code, GitOps, instant rollback), elasticity (spin up another LB instance in seconds when traffic spikes), and cost (commodity EC2 + open-source software is dramatically cheaper per connection than an F5). Google's Maglev is the canonical proof point — a software packet processor running on standard Linux servers that handles Google's entire ingress traffic, tens of millions of packets per second per node. The trade-off: hardware LBs still win on raw per-box throughput and predictable latency for the highest-traffic sites, but the gap narrows every year as DPDK and XDP let software hit 10Gbps+ on cheap NICs.
**Visual:**
```
Hardware (F5):                Software (NGINX/Envoy):
+----------+                  +--------+   +--------+
| F5 box   | <== ASIC         | nginx  |   | nginx  |
| $250k    |     fast, rigid  | x86 EC2|...| x86 EC2|
+----------+                  +--------+   +--------+
  months to buy                 seconds to spin
```

### Q3. Why does a load balancer need health checks, and what happens if they are misconfigured?
**Answer:** Without health checks, a load balancer blindly forwards traffic to backends that may be dead, GC-paused, or returning 500s — actively making availability worse than no balancer at all. Health checks (HTTP `GET /healthz`, TCP connect, custom script) probe each backend on a fixed interval and remove failing ones from rotation until they recover. The misconfigurations are well-known: too-aggressive checks (1-second interval, 1-failure threshold) flap healthy backends in and out during routine GC pauses, causing cascading retries; too-relaxed checks (60-second interval) leave a dead instance receiving traffic for minutes. AWS ALB's defaults — 30-second interval, healthy threshold 5, unhealthy threshold 2 — reflect a balance: a hard crash is detected in 60–90 seconds, and a brief pause does not trigger drain. Netflix's Eureka goes further with self-registration: backends register themselves on boot and send heartbeats every 30 seconds; missing heartbeats for 90 seconds triggers eviction, decoupling detection from the balancer itself.
**Visual:**
```
Aggressive (flap):        Balanced:                Lazy (slow):
1s interval              10s interval              60s interval
1 fail = drain           3 fails = drain           5 fails = drain
=> B1 in/out/in/out      => B1 dies, drained       => B1 dead, traffic
   chaos                    cleanly in ~30s            continues for ~5 min
```

### Q4. What are the main load-balancing algorithms, and how do you choose between them?
**Answer:** The five canonical algorithms are: **round-robin** (rotate sequentially, assumes equal backends), **weighted round-robin** (proportional to capacity, used when backends differ in size), **least-connections** (pick fewest in-flight, default for variable-length requests like video transcodes), **IP-hash / consistent hash** (sticky routing for session affinity or sharded backends), and **latency-based / peak EWMA** (route around slow backends, popularized by Finagle). The choice depends on three questions: Are backends equal-capacity? (If not, use weighted.) Are request lengths variable? (If yes, use least-connections to avoid pile-up on the slow one.) Does the backend hold per-client state? (If yes, use consistent hashing so the same client lands on the same box.) Are some backends intermittently slow? (If yes, latency-based will route around them.) NGINX defaults to round-robin because it is "good enough" for homogeneous fleets; Twitter's Finagle defaults to latency-based EWMA because their backends have wildly variable GC behavior. There is no universal best — pick the one whose assumptions match your fleet.
**Visual:**
```
Equal backends, equal reqs -> Round Robin
Unequal backends           -> Weighted Round Robin
Variable req length        -> Least Connections
Per-client state           -> IP Hash / Consistent
Variable backend latency   -> Latency (EWMA)
```

### Q5. How does a load balancer itself avoid becoming a single point of failure?
**Answer:** A load balancer is itself a distributed system that must be highly available, or it just moves the SPOF from the backend to the front door. The standard pattern is **redundant pairs with VIP failover**: two LB instances share a Virtual IP via VRRP or keepalived; one is active, the other hot-standby, and if the active dies the standby claims the VIP within sub-second ARP announcement. Cloud providers operationalize this differently — AWS ELB/ALB/NLB is a managed service that internally runs multiple nodes across Availability Zones, exposing one DNS name that automatically fails over. Netflix runs multiple Zuul instances behind AWS Network Load Balancer, and Zuul itself uses Eureka to find backend instances; if a Zuul node dies, the NLB routes around it. The deeper pattern is **layered load balancing**: DNS-based global LB (Route 53, Cloudflare) at the top, regional Anycast LB in the middle, per-AZ software LB at the bottom — each layer is itself HA, and no single failure can take the service down. The rule: every load balancer in production must have a redundant peer or be a managed service with internal redundancy.
**Visual:**
```
DNS (Route 53) ---> VIP --+--> LB-A (active)  --> backends
                          |
                          +--> LB-B (standby) --> backends
                                  ^
                                  VIP claim if A dies (VRRP/ARP)
```

### Q6. What is the difference between client-side load balancing and server-side load balancing?
**Answer:** **Server-side** load balancing is the classic model: clients talk to a VIP, a dedicated LB appliance or process forwards to backends. The LB is a separate hop, adding latency and operational surface, but clients stay simple and the algorithm is centralized. **Client-side** load balancing moves the selection into the caller: the client knows the full list of backends (via a service registry like Consul, Eureka, or Kubernetes Endpoints) and picks one directly per request, eliminating the extra hop. Netflix's Ribbon, gRPC's client-side LB, and Envoy's sidecar mode are all client-side patterns. The trade-off: server-side is easier to reason about and works for any client (including curl), while client-side is lower-latency and avoids the LB as a bottleneck, but requires every client to embed the LB logic and registry integration. Service mesh architectures (Istio, Linkerd) blend both — the sidecar proxy is technically server-side from the application's view but client-side from the network's view, giving you the latency wins without polluting application code. The modern default for internal microservice traffic is client-side or sidecar; for external ingress it remains server-side.
**Visual:**
```
Server-side:                Client-side:
Client -> LB -> backend     Client -> [embedded LB] -> backend
        (extra hop)                  (no hop, needs registry)
```

### Q7. What is "draining" a backend, and why does it matter during deploys?
**Answer:** Draining is the process of gracefully removing a backend from the load balancer's rotation without dropping in-flight requests. The balancer stops sending new connections to the drained backend but lets existing ones finish; once the in-flight count reaches zero, the backend can be safely terminated or replaced. This matters during deploys because killing a backend mid-request — say, halfway through a 5-second video transcode or a 2-second database write — causes user-visible errors and 500s. AWS ALB's deregistration delay (default 300 seconds) implements this: deregistered targets keep receiving responses for in-flight requests until they complete or the timeout fires. Kubernetes does the same with `preStop` hooks and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`. Without draining, every deploy is a small outage; with draining, deploys are invisible to users even at high traffic. Netflix's red/black deploys go further — bring up the new version, shift traffic 1% → 10% → 100%, drain the old version, then terminate — and the entire flow is driven by the load balancer's weighting API.
**Visual:**
```
1. B3 is healthy, receiving traffic
2. Deploy starts: LB sets B3 weight=0 (DRAINING)
   - no new connections
   - existing conns finish (in_flight -> 0)
3. B3 reaches in_flight=0 -> safe to kill
4. B3 replaced with new version, re-added (weight -> 1)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run an e-commerce site with one backend server handling 1,000 RPS. Traffic is projected to grow 20× over the next six months. How do you architect for this?
**Answer:** First, recognize that 20,000 RPS from a single box is not feasible — even a maxed-out EC2 instance tops out around 5,000–10,000 RPS for typical web workloads. The architecture is: provision N backend instances behind a managed load balancer (AWS ALB), where N is sized to handle 20,000 RPS at ~60% CPU headroom. With each box handling ~2,000 RPS comfortably, you need ~10 instances, plus 2–3 for failure margin. Wire the ALB to an Auto Scaling Group that scales on CPU and request-count-per-target, so traffic spikes spin up new instances automatically. Add Route 53 health-checked multi-AZ failover for DNS-level resilience. Use least-connections routing because product-detail and checkout requests have variable lengths. Put a CDN (CloudFront) in front for static assets and cacheable catalog pages to reduce RPS to the origin by 80–90%. Add Redis for session state so any backend can serve any user (no stickiness required). The result: a horizontally scalable, self-healing fleet where growth is a config change in the autoscaler, not a hardware refresh.
**Visual:**
```
Route53 (DNS failover, multi-AZ)
   |
   v
CloudFront (CDN, cache 80% of reads)
   |
   v
AWS ALB (least-connections, health checks)
   |
   +---> ASG: 10-13 EC2 instances across 3 AZs
   |        |
   |        v
   +---> Redis (session store, shared)
   |
   v
RDS Postgres (multi-AZ primary + read replicas)
```

### Q2. Your load balancer is sending traffic to a backend that is returning 500 errors, but the health check endpoint returns 200. How do you detect and handle this?
**Answer:** This is the classic "shallow health check" failure: the `/healthz` endpoint works, but the actual request path is broken — perhaps the database connection pool is exhausted, a downstream dependency is timing out, or a recent deploy corrupted a config. The fix has two parts. First, make the health check **deep**: have `/healthz` actually exercise the critical path — open a DB connection, ping Redis, call a downstream service — and return 200 only if all pass. Netflix's "cassandra-health" check is exactly this pattern. Second, add **outlier detection** at the LB layer: modern balancers like Envoy and Istio support automatic outlier detection, where a backend returning 5xx above a threshold (say, 5% over 1 minute) is ejected from rotation for a quarantine period even if `/healthz` says 200. AWS ALB has similar "target health" status logic. Operationally, set up alerts on per-backend 5xx rates so the on-call is paged when one box is misbehaving, and use canary deploys so a bad deploy is caught at 1% traffic before it affects the whole fleet.
**Visual:**
```
Shallow:  /healthz -> 200 (but /checkout -> 500)
Deep:     /healthz -> 200 ONLY IF db+redis+downstream all OK
Outlier:  LB ejects backend if 5xx rate > 5% for 60s,
          regardless of /healthz result
```

### Q3. You have 100 backend instances behind an AWS ALB. During a deploy, you take 50 of them out at once to update. Half your users see 500s. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** You violated the **rolling deploy** rule: never take more backends out of rotation than you have spare capacity to absorb. With 100 instances at, say, 60% average CPU, removing 50 instantly doubles the load on the remaining 50 to 120% — they saturate, queue requests, and start returning 500s or timing out. The fix is a proper rolling deploy: take out batches of 10% (10 instances) at a time, deploy, verify health, then move to the next batch — total deploy takes longer but no user is ever affected. Better still, use a **blue/green or canary** deploy: bring up 50 new instances alongside the 50 old ones, shift traffic 10% → 50% → 100% over 10 minutes via ALB weighted target groups, then drain and terminate the old. Set the ALB deregistration delay to a value longer than your longest request (default 300s is usually fine). Add a "soak" period between batches — 5 minutes at the new version — to catch regressions. The principle: capacity is `healthy_backends × per_backend_capacity`; a deploy that drops below current demand will fail, period.
**Visual:**
```
WRONG:                     RIGHT (rolling 10%):
T0: 100 old, 0 new         T0: 100 old, 0 new
T1: 50 old, 0 new  <- OOM  T1: 90 old + 10 new
T2: 50 new                 T2: 80 old + 20 new (verify)
                          ... T10: 0 old + 100 new
```

### Q4. Your service has sticky sessions enabled (IP-hash) and one backend is receiving 80% of traffic while others are idle. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** This is **hashing skew** — IP-hash distribution depends on the input distribution, and a small number of high-volume clients (or a NAT-ing corporate proxy that funnels thousands of users through one source IP) can hash to the same backend. The result: one backend is hot, the rest idle, and the hot one is on the edge of failure. Diagnose by checking per-backend request rates and the distribution of source IPs — if the top 1% of IPs generate 80% of traffic, you have a NAT/proxy concentration problem. Fixes, in order of preference: (1) **stop using IP-hash** if you don't actually need stickiness — move to least-connections or round-robin and store session state externally in Redis so any backend can serve any user; (2) if stickiness is mandatory (e.g., backend holds in-memory session), use **consistent hashing with virtual nodes** (200+ vnodes per backend) so the hash ring distributes more evenly; (3) hash on a session cookie instead of source IP, so the load is spread across cookie values; (4) cap any single backend's load with a circuit breaker that spills overflow to the next backend in the ring. Netflix's EVCache-based session store is the canonical enabler of "any backend serves any user."
**Visual:**
```
IP-hash skew:                  Consistent hash w/ vnodes:
client_A -> B3 (80% load)      ring: [v1,v2,...,v200] x N backends
client_B -> B3                  client_A hashes between v47(B2),v48(B5)
client_C -> B3                  -> more even distribution
others   -> B1, B2, B4 (idle)   -> hot-spot resistance up to 1/N
```

### Q5. You are designing a global API that must serve 99.99% availability. How does load balancing fit into the architecture?
**Answer:** 99.99% availability is ~52 minutes of downtime per year — you cannot achieve it with a single load balancer or a single region. The architecture is layered. **Layer 1 — Global DNS**: Route 53 or Cloudflare with health-checked multi-region failover records; if a region's LB stops responding to health checks, DNS flips to another region within 60 seconds (TTL-bounded). **Layer 2 — Anycast / global LB**: AWS Global Accelerator or Cloudflare's Anycast IPs give users a single IP that routes to the nearest healthy region at the network layer, sub-second failover. **Layer 3 — Regional LB**: each region runs an ALB or NLB across at least 3 AZs, with redundant nodes managed by the cloud provider. **Layer 4 — Backend fleet**: an ASG per AZ, sized for 50% capacity loss (one AZ gone) at peak. **Layer 5 — Application**: circuit breakers (Resilience4j, Hystrix) so a failing dependency doesn't cascade. Multi-region active-active (Netflix runs three regions) gives you the final nines. The math: one region at 99.9% × 3 active regions with independent failure modes ≈ 99.9999% theoretical. The cost is enormous, which is why 99.99% is the typical ceiling for non-mission-critical products and 99.999% is reserved for payments, emergency, and telecom.
**Visual:**
```
Route 53 (DNS health check, 60s failover)
   |
   v
Global Accelerator (Anycast IP, sub-second failover)
   |
   +--> us-east-1 ALB (3 AZs, ASG x 20 each)
   +--> eu-west-1 ALB (3 AZs, ASG x 20 each)
   +--> ap-southeast-1 ALB (3 AZs, ASG x 20 each)
              each region: independent failure mode
              active-active, geo-routed by latency
```

### Q6. You migrate from a single NGINX box to AWS ALB and now see higher p99 latency. Why, and what do you do?
**Answer:** AWS ALB is a managed multi-tenant service; its per-request latency includes a network hop to the ALB's internal nodes, and during scale events or noisy-neighbor traffic it can show variable queuing that hits p99. NGINX on a dedicated EC2 box had a single hop with predictable CPU. To diagnose: first, measure where the latency is added — break the request into client→ALB, ALB→target, target→response, and compare against your old NGINX path. If the ALB→target segment is the culprit, check whether your targets are in the same AZ as the ALB node (cross-AZ hops add 1–2 ms); enable ALB's "cross-zone load balancing off" if you want AZ-local routing, or "on" if you want even distribution. If targets are healthy but p99 is still high, you may be hitting ALB's per-connection rate smoothing — pre-warm the ALB by opening idle connections before a known spike (AWS support can pre-provision capacity for predictable events like Black Friday). Consider switching to **NLB** if you don't need L7 features — NLB is faster (passes TCP through, no HTTP parsing) and has more predictable latency. Finally, if p99 is genuinely ALB-induced and your traffic justifies it, run your own Envoy or NGINX on EC2 for the hot path, and let ALB handle the rest — hybrid is fine.
**Visual:**
```
Old:  client -> NGINX (1 hop, 0.5ms)  -> backend
New:  client -> ALB (multi-tenant) -> backend
                    ^- can add 1-5ms p99 under load
Fix:  same-AZ targets, NLB for hot path, or self-hosted Envoy
```

### Q7. Your Kubernetes service has 10 Pods. You scale to 100 Pods for a traffic spike, but clients still see errors for 30 seconds. Why?
**Answer:** Kubernetes Service → Endpoints → Pods is eventually consistent, and the lag between "Pod is ready" and "kube-proxy has programmed iptables/IPVS to send it traffic" can be 5–30 seconds depending on the kube-proxy mode, the controller's sync interval, and iptables rule propagation. During that window, the load balancer (whether kube-proxy or an external cloud LB integrated via the Service `type: LoadBalancer`) may not have all 100 new backends in rotation, so traffic concentrates on the original 10 — which then saturate and start erroring. Fixes: (1) ensure Pods report `ready` only after they are genuinely ready to serve (proper `readinessProbe` with `initialDelaySeconds` and `failureThreshold`); (2) use `preStop` hooks that sleep for a few seconds to give kube-proxy time to deregister before the Pod actually terminates; (3) on scale-up, set a `readinessGates` if you have external health signals; (4) switch kube-proxy from `iptables` mode to `IPVS` mode — IPVS syncs faster and handles large endpoint lists better; (5) for external LB, configure the cloud controller's `service.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-health-check-*` annotations to match your app's actual readiness. The deeper fix is to over-provision slightly so even partial routing doesn't saturate the visible backends during the sync window.
**Visual:**
```
T0: 10 Pods in Endpoints, all serving
T1: scale to 100; Pods booting
T2: 50 Pods ready, BUT kube-proxy hasn't synced iptables
    -> traffic still goes to 10 Pods -> saturation -> errors
T3: kube-proxy syncs (5-30s lag) -> 60 Pods in rotation -> healthy
Fix: readinessProbe + preStop + IPVS mode
```
